    Zomo’s cultural notebook

    Specific traditions, people and objects. Cultural motifs are distinct from dated political flags. Dates below describe checked evidence, not the invention of a tradition.

    In documented Hausa storytelling, Zomo the hare and Gizo the spider are distinct recurring characters. Taswira’s Zomo is a new fictional guide.       Everything on the map, scene by scene, with its sources. Built 2026-11-26. While the map plays, moving sparks, dust, light and ripples are decoration: only the dots, lines, colours and text carry information.

      Deep time: how the land was made (600 million to 5,000 years ago)

      Before there were people, the land itself moved. This chapter covers about 600 million years in a few minutes: the continents gather and break apart, a rift opens into West Africa and stops, the Niger Delta grows, volcanoes rise, the Sahara is born, and it turns green and dries again. If those 600 million years were one day, everything since the first Nok farmers would fit into its last half-second.

      How to read this map. The continents are drawn where a published plate model puts them (Merdith et al. 2021), on a globe with the grid of latitude and longitude of the time. The outlines are today's continents with their shelves, simplified, so they show where the land was, not the coastlines of the time. Rocks record how far from the poles they formed but not how far east or west, so the longitudes of deep time are the model's choice. The last four scenes are on the plain map of today's land, lakes and rivers. A volcano is one cone symbol for every volcano or volcanic field. The glow, smoke, sand, grass and moving water drawn over the map are decoration, not measurements.

      about 600 to 530 million years ago: Africa inside Gondwana

      About 600 million years ago, the rock that is now Nigeria lay inside a growing supercontinent called Gondwana. Between about 600 and 530 million years ago, mountain building welded its pieces together: South America, Africa, Antarctica, Arabia, India and Australia. Africa and South America sat side by side. Watch where Nigeria's rock goes from here.

      about 200 to 160 million years ago: Pangaea breaks up

      Gondwana had joined the northern continents into one supercontinent, Pangaea. About 200 million years ago, huge volcanic eruptions marked the start of its break-up, and the Central Atlantic opened between north-west Africa and North America. Between about 180 and 160 million years ago, Africa and Antarctica began to part.

      about 150 to 100 million years ago: The South Atlantic opens

      Then South America and Africa pulled apart like a zip opening from the south. The rift spread north from about 150 or 140 million years ago, and new ocean floor formed from about 135 to 130 million years ago. North of the equator, where Nigeria's coast is now, rifting began after about 120 million years ago and went on until about 100 million years ago.

      Disputed: Sources disagree on when the last land link broke: dinosaur footprints suggest some connection until about 120 million years ago, while rifting north of the equator went on until about 100 to 96 million years ago. The page shows the whole range.

      about 145 to 84 million years ago: A rift that stopped: the Benue Trough

      As the two continents parted, a third arm of the rift opened into Africa: the Benue Trough, about 1,000 km long, from the Bight of Benin to Lake Chad. It began to open at the start of the Cretaceous, about 145 million years ago, then stopped while the other two arms went on to become the South Atlantic. About 84 million years ago it was squeezed and folded. The Benue River runs along it today.

      around 70 million years ago: Coal swamps

      Around 70 million years ago, brackish marshes spread at the southern end of the trough, in the Anambra Basin. Their plants were buried and slowly became coal. It is the coal of the Udi Hills around Enugu, first shipped to Britain by 1914.

      about 66 million years ago to today: Fire from below: Africa's volcanoes

      1. about 66 million years ago to today. Africa's volcanoes rise where its plates are stretching apart, or where hot rock wells up from deep inside the Earth.
      2. from about 66 or about 30 million years ago: sources differ. In the west, a line of volcanoes runs from the Gulf of Guinea inland. Nigeria's Biu Plateau is linked to it, and Mount Cameroon is its most active volcano.
      3. about 31 to 29 million years ago. About 30 million years ago, floods of lava poured out in Ethiopia, most of them within about a million years, and built the Ethiopian highlands.
      4. about 2.5 million years ago. In the East African Rift, Kilimanjaro began to grow about two and a half million years ago.
      5. 1999 to 2021. In recent decades Mount Cameroon erupted in 1999, 2000 and 2012, and the runny lava of Nyiragongo reached the city of Goma in 2002 and 2021, killing people and forcing many to flee.

      Disputed: Sources differ on when the Cameroon line began: a plume under the Oku area since about 66 million years ago, or the line's development from around 30 million years ago. Death tolls for Nyiragongo's eruptions also differ, so none are given.

      • Biu Plateau (Volcano or volcanic field). A volcanic plateau in north-eastern Nigeria. Some geologists link its volcanoes to the Cameroon line to the south. Evidence: Geology (secondary sources). Location: Placed at the town of Biu, on the plateau. The volcanic field is wider and is not drawn. How sure: Approximate. Sources: Biu Plateau (Wikipedia), Coordinates of the volcanoes in the deep-time chapter (Wikipedia place articles).
      • Mount Cameroon (Volcano or volcanic field). The most active volcano of the Cameroon line, close to the sea. It erupted from its flanks in 1999 and 2000, when the lava came within about 200 m of the sea, and briefly in 2012. Evidence: Geology and eruption records (secondary sources). Location: The summit, from a gazetteer. How sure: Firm. Sources: Mount Cameroon (Wikipedia), Coordinates of the volcanoes in the deep-time chapter (Wikipedia place articles).
      • Ethiopian flood basalts (Volcano or volcanic field). Around 30 million years ago, floods of lava poured out here, most of them within about a million years, and built up the Ethiopian highlands. The eruptions are thought to mark hot rock rising from deep in the Earth, the Afar plume. Evidence: Geology (peer-reviewed dating). Location: A point on the Ethiopian plateau. The lava covered a much wider area, which is not drawn. How sure: Approximate. Sources: Timing of the Ethiopian flood basalt event and implications for plume birth and global change, Coordinates of the volcanoes in the deep-time chapter (Wikipedia place articles).
      • Kilimanjaro (Volcano or volcanic field). Three volcanic centres beside the East African Rift. Activity began about 2.5 million years ago at Shira and later moved east to Mawenzi and Kibo. Kibo, the summit cone, is dormant rather than extinct. Evidence: Geology (peer-reviewed dating, seen through summaries). Location: The summit, from a gazetteer. How sure: Firm. Sources: New K-Ar age determinations of Kilimanjaro volcano in the North Tanzanian diverging rift, East Africa, Coordinates of the volcanoes in the deep-time chapter (Wikipedia place articles).
      • Nyiragongo (Volcano or volcanic field). A volcano above the city of Goma, in the western branch of the East African Rift. Its lava is unusually runny: in 1977 it ran down the upper slopes at up to 60 km/h. In 2002 and 2021 lava reached Goma. Sources give different numbers of people killed and displaced, so none are given here. Evidence: Eruption records (secondary sources). Location: The summit, from a gazetteer. How sure: Firm. Sources: Mount Nyiragongo (Wikipedia), Volcano Watch: Central African metropolis again threatened by looming volcanic eruption, Coordinates of the volcanoes in the deep-time chapter (Wikipedia place articles).

      about 56 million years ago to today: The Niger Delta grows

      From about 56 million years ago, at the start of the Eocene, the Niger and the Benue carried sand and mud to the sea where the arms of the old rift met. The delta has built out about 250 km to the south-west, over the ocean floor, and now covers some 300,000 km². Its sediment is more than 10 km thick, and it is still growing.

      • Niger Delta. Since the Eocene, which began about 56 million years ago, the Niger and Benue have carried sand and mud to the sea here. The delta has built out about 250 km to the south-west over the ocean floor, to some 300,000 km², with sediment more than 10 km thick. It sits where the arms of the old rift met. Evidence: Geology (government survey report). Location: A point on today's delta. The coast and rivers are drawn as they are today; when the delta began, the shore was further inland. How sure: Firm. Sources: Tertiary Niger Delta (Akata-Agbada) Petroleum System, Niger Delta Province (Open-File Report 99-50-H, chapter A), Eocene (Wikipedia).

      Sources: Tertiary Niger Delta (Akata-Agbada) Petroleum System, Niger Delta Province (Open-File Report 99-50-H, chapter A), Eocene (Wikipedia).

      about 11 to 7 million years ago: The Sahara is born

      The Sahara has a beginning. Wind-blown dune sand about 7 million years old, found in the northern Chad Basin, is the oldest known sign of a desert there. Before that find, most geologists thought the desert was only 2 to 3 million years old. A later study links the drying to the shrinking of the Tethys Sea, between about 11 and 7 million years ago.

      Disputed: Not all researchers accept the early date or the Tethys explanation.

      • Northern Chad Basin. Where wind-blown dune sand about 7 million years old was found: the oldest known sign of a desert in the Sahara. Evidence: Geology (peer-reviewed article). Location: A point in the northern Chad Basin, as the sources describe it. The find spot is not drawn; the dashed ring shows the uncertainty. How sure: Approximate. Sources: The Age of the Sahara Desert.

      Sources: The Age of the Sahara Desert, Climate simulation doubles Sahara's age.

      about 14,500 to 5,000 years ago: A green Sahara, then the desert returns

      From about 14,500 years ago, stronger monsoon rains turned the Sahara green, with grassland, lakes and rivers, and Lake Chad grew into a vast Lake Mega-Chad. The rains weakened between about 6,000 and 5,000 years ago, in steps and at different times in different places. In the eastern Sahara, archaeology shows people leaving the drying desert for the Nile valley and moving south towards today's Sahel. South of Lake Chad, farming and herding villages spread from about 1800 BCE. Whether people from the drying desert moved there is not shown by the sources checked so far.

      • Lake Mega-Chad (Lake). In wet periods Lake Chad was far larger than today, and drained to the Benue and the Niger through the Mayo Kebbi. Halo or field: A disc of 330,000 km², the smaller of the two sizes given, centred on today's Lake Chad. The lake's real shoreline is not drawn. Evidence: Geology and climate studies (secondary sources). Location: Centred on today's Lake Chad. Disputed: Its size is given as about 330,000 km² in one source and about 400,000 km² in another. How sure: Disputed. Sources: African humid period (Wikipedia), Coordinates and facts for the deep-time chapter (Wikipedia place articles).

      Sources: African humid period (Wikipedia), Climate-Controlled Holocene Occupation in the Sahara: Motor of Africa's Evolution, Burial Practices, Settlement and Regional Connections around the Southern Lake Chad Basin, 1500 BC-AD 1500, Coordinates and facts for the deep-time chapter (Wikipedia place articles).

      Africa: peoples, cities and kingdoms (about 300,000 years ago to 1495 CE · overview, then rewind)

      A continental tour before the close-up. Each stop is a selected dated moment, not a claim about a whole kingdom’s duration. The last five views change geographic scale, then the story rewinds to Nok.

      How to read this map. Points locate sites or city centres with stated uncertainty, never empire outlines. Architecture is an original symbolic schematic, not a scale reconstruction or an emblem. Geography and the river locator are generalised modern physical references, not ancient coastlines, riverbanks or lake extents. Capital identifications and dates remain qualified. The tour explicitly jumps and rewinds; its progress rail shows scene order, not proportional years.

      About 300,000 years ago: Our species has an African story

      Rewind: the previous chapter ended around 5,000 years ago. Now we return to roughly 300,000 years ago. At Jebel Irhoud, early Homo sapiens remains were found with Middle Stone Age tools. This is one part of a much wider African story of human origins.

      • Jebel Irhoud · approximate locality. At Jebel Irhoud in present-day Morocco, early Homo sapiens remains occur with Middle Stone Age tools dated to about 300,000 years ago. This is one part of a much wider African story of human origins. Evidence: Archaeology and institutional/scholarly records. Location: Approximate fossil locality based on a nearby landmark, rounded to 31.87 N, 8.87 W. The 15 km overview halo is illustrative, not surveyed excavation accuracy. How sure: Approximate. Sources: The first of our kind, The age of the hominin fossils from Jebel Irhoud, Morocco, and the origins of the Middle Stone Age, Djebel Irhoud fossil locality 82672.

      Sources: The first of our kind, The age of the hominin fossils from Jebel Irhoud, Morocco, and the origins of the Middle Stone Age, Djebel Irhoud fossil locality 82672.

      Around 3100 BCE: A state takes shape on the Nile

      Jump forward by almost 300,000 years. Around 3100 BCE, the gradual unification of Upper and Lower Egypt reached a major stage. Memphis became a capital between the two regions.

Evidence: Archaeology and institutional/scholarly records. Location: UNESCO property component 86-001 representative point How sure: Approximate. Sources: Early Dynastic Period, Memphis and its Necropolis — Maps / geographical data.

      Third century BCE: Kush builds its own royal landscape

      Further south on the Nile, Meroe was a major centre of Kush. In the third century BCE, royal burials here used steep-sided pyramids above underground tombs. The city and its royal cemeteries formed distinct parts of this landscape.

      • Meroe · royal cemeteries. Meroe was a major centre of Kush. From the third century BCE, most Kushite rulers were buried here. Its royal cemeteries used steep-sided pyramids above tombs cut into the ground. Schematic: Original symbolic steep-sided royal funerary pyramid with chapel. Represents the documented third-century BCE burial phase, not a measured or individually dated tomb. The assembled cemetery is an architectural illustration: numbers, arrangement and reveal order are symbolic. Evidence: Archaeology and institutional/scholarly records. Location: Representative point of the royal cemetery complex, separate from the royal city. It does not locate an individual pyramid footprint. How sure: Approximate. Sources: Archaeological Sites of the Island of Meroe, Archaeological Sites of the Island of Meroe — Nomination Text, Sudanese Cultural Heritage Sites.

      Sources: Archaeological Sites of the Island of Meroe, Archaeological Sites of the Island of Meroe — Nomination Text, Sudanese Cultural Heritage Sites.

      Around 200 BCE · within a longer urban sequence: A town without an invented king

      Shift west to the inland Niger delta. Djenné-Djenno grew from about 250 BCE. Archaeology reveals crafts, exchange and forms of self-government: an urban history alongside the stories of kings and courts.

      • Djenné-Djenno — ancient town. At Djenné-Djenno, a town grew in the inland Niger delta from about 250 BCE. Archaeology reveals crafts, exchange, and forms of self-government. Evidence: Archaeology and institutional/scholarly records. Location: Use a point with a broad site marker; no surveyed boundary or palace position established here. How sure: Approximate. Sources: Old Towns of Djenné, Sahel: Art and Empires on the Shores of the Sahara — Inside the Exhibition, Old Towns of Djenné — Maps, geographical data.

      Third–fourth centuries CE: Stone becomes architecture

      In north-eastern Africa, Aksum’s great stone stelae were carved in the third and fourth centuries CE. Some turned a single block of stone into the image of a many-storeyed building.

      Around 1100 CE · selected trade context: Gold, exchange and an uncertain capital

      Thirteenth century CE · regional overview: A centre east of Lake Chad

      Now east of Lake Chad. Kanem linked communities across the Sahara. Recent archaeological work considers Tié a probable location of Njimi, an early Islamic capital. The identification remains a research question as the regional story comes into focus.

      Disputed: Tié’s identification with Njimi is probable, not certain. No unverified capital point or medieval lake shoreline is drawn.

      Sources: The Lake Chad Region as a Crossroads: first archaeological and oral historical investigations into early Kanem-Borno and its intra-African connections, New Luminescence and Radiocarbon Dates for Kanem-Borno Fired-Brick Elite Sites in Kanem, Chad: Bayesian Chronological Modelling of Settlement Construction, Publication: Archaeological research in Tié, Chad.

      1324 CE · Musa’s pilgrimage: Mali, Musa and a city of learning

      In 1324, Mali’s ruler Musa travelled to Mecca through Cairo. His patronage helped Timbuktu develop as a centre of Islamic study. Timbuktu enters this tour as a commercial and scholarly city.

      • Mali — Musa's 1324 pilgrimage and Timbuktu. In 1324, Mali's ruler Musa travelled to Mecca through Cairo. His patronage helped Timbuktu develop as a centre of Islamic study. Evidence: Archaeology and institutional/scholarly records. Location: Property-level point, not a verified medieval palace, market stall, or exact initial mosque footprint. How sure: Approximate. Sources: Sahel: Art and Empires on the Shores of the Sahara — Inside the Exhibition, Timbuktu.

      Sources: Sahel: Art and Empires on the Shores of the Sahara — Inside the Exhibition, Timbuktu.

      Around 1400 CE · later building phase: A city built in stone

      What makes a city? Look beyond its most famous tower. Above the settlement, stone enclosures and terraces follow the granite hill. Below it, the Great Enclosure reveals the skill of its stone builders. An inner wall creates a narrow passage toward the conical tower. Around these monuments were spaces for living, including dhaka houses and granaries. A city was more than its monuments. People made it a place to live.

      • Great Zimbabwe · enclosure. In southern Africa, Great Zimbabwe grew into a major trading city. Its fourteenth-century Great Enclosure still expresses the skill of its stone builders.       Thirteenth–fourteenth centuries CE: Africa faces the Indian Ocean too

      Turn toward the Indian Ocean. Kilwa Kisiwani flourished as a Swahili trading city in the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries. Its sea connections belong in Africa’s history alongside the Sahara and the Niger.

Its merchants connected African hinterland goods with Indian Ocean markets in Arabia, India and China. Evidence: Archaeology and institutional/scholarly records. Location: Kilwa Kisiwani component 144-001 representative point How sure: Approximate.       1495 CE · monument at Gao: Gao and the Songhai world

      Rewind · about 1500 BCE: Rewind to the first Nok chapter

      Our continental tour reached the medieval centuries. Now rewind to about 1500 BCE. We will follow the much earlier farmers, sculptors and ironworkers associated with Nok, then build the later regional story in order.

      • Nok village (Jaba LGA, Kaduna State). The first known Nok terracotta was found here in 1928, about 7 m deep in a tin mine. A second head, found nearby in 1943, led Bernard Fagg to recognise a lost sculptural tradition, and the culture is named after the village. Evidence: Documented chance finds, later studied by archaeologists. Location: Town location. The finds came from tin mines near the village. How sure: Firm. Sources: Nok culture (Wikipedia), Coordinates of Nok (Jaba LGA), Kagarko and Katsina-Ala (Wikipedia place articles).

      Nok: farmers, sculptors and early iron (about 1500 BCE to the turn of the era)

      The Nok culture lived in the hills and valleys of central Nigeria, roughly between today's Abuja, Kaduna and Jos. It is known from archaeology alone: no written records survive, so everything here comes from excavated sites and radiocarbon dates.

      about 1500 BCE to 1 CE: Where the Nok lived

      Archaeologists have found almost 500 Nok sites across central Nigeria and excavated 84 of them, with 270 radiocarbon dates. The four places on the map are ones named in the sources checked for this page. They are examples, not a full map of Nok sites.

      • Nok village (Jaba LGA, Kaduna State). The first known Nok terracotta was found here in 1928, about 7 m deep in a tin mine. A second head, found nearby in 1943, led Bernard Fagg to recognise a lost sculptural tradition, and the culture is named after the village. Evidence: Documented chance finds, later studied by archaeologists. Location: Town location. The finds came from tin mines near the village. How sure: Firm. Sources: Nok culture (Wikipedia), Coordinates of Nok (Jaba LGA), Kagarko and Katsina-Ala (Wikipedia place articles).
      • Janruwa, Janjala and Akura, near Kagarko. Three Nok sites about 1 km apart, excavated by the Frankfurt Nok project. They yielded pottery, terracotta fragments and plant remains used to study what Nok farmers grew. Evidence: Excavated (Frankfurt Nok project). Location: Placed at Kagarko town. The sites are near the town, not at this exact point. How sure: Firm. Sources: Exploring the Nok enigma, Coordinates of Nok (Jaba LGA), Kagarko and Katsina-Ala (Wikipedia place articles).
      • Taruga. A valley near the village of Takushara, excavated for eight days by Bernard Fagg in January 1961. Iron objects, slag, fragments of furnace blowpipes (tuyères) and pottery were found, and these finds led archaeologists to class the Nok culture as Iron Age. Evidence: Excavated (Fagg, 1961). Location: Rough. Placed 60 km south-east of Abuja from a written description, and could be 20 to 30 km out. The ring shows that uncertainty. Disputed: The date of Taruga's iron working is given as about 600 BCE in some histories, but Fagg's radiocarbon dates point to about the 4th to 3rd centuries BCE. The Frankfurt project places Nok iron working in the middle of the first millennium BCE. How sure: Disputed. Sources: Nok culture (Wikipedia), Taruga (Wikipedia), Development of complex societies in sub-Saharan Africa: The Nigerian Nok Culture (project results).
      • Katsina-Ala (Benue State). Terracotta heads and figures found here in the mid-20th century resemble Nok work. Fagg described them as a distinctive sub-style, far to the south-east of Nok village. Evidence: Chance finds described in secondary sources. Location: Town location. The exact find spots are not given in the sources checked. Disputed: Whether these are Nok proper or a related tradition is not settled in the sources checked. How sure: Disputed. Sources: Coordinates of Nok (Jaba LGA), Kagarko and Katsina-Ala (Wikipedia place articles).

      Sources: Development of complex societies in sub-Saharan Africa: The Nigerian Nok Culture (project results).

      about 1500 to 900 BCE: First farmers

      The earliest evidence of Nok farming dates to around 1500 BCE. Communities mainly grew millet. This phase is known from pottery and plant remains, not from sculpture: the terracottas came about six centuries later.

      • Janruwa, Janjala and Akura, near Kagarko. Three Nok sites about 1 km apart, excavated by the Frankfurt Nok project. The sites are near the town, not at this exact point. How sure: Firm. Sources: Exploring the Nok enigma, Coordinates of Nok (Jaba LGA), Kagarko and Katsina-Ala (Wikipedia place articles).

      Sources: Development of complex societies in sub-Saharan Africa: The Nigerian Nok Culture (project results), Professor Peter Breunig: The Significance of Nok Culture Sculptures in Nigerian Prehistory.

      about 900 to 400 BCE: Villages grow and sculpture begins

      Around 900 BCE settlements suddenly became much denser, and people began making large clay sculptures of human heads and figures. Many were deliberately broken and deposited, some near graves, at sites such as Pangwari and Ifana. Sculpture production seems to fall off sharply around 400 BCE.

      1928 to 2021: Archaeological research and looting

      Tin-mining finds in 1928 and 1943 brought the sculptures to archaeologists' attention. Fagg excavated Taruga in 1961, and the Frankfurt project worked systematically from 2005 to 2021. When German researchers began looking for Nok sites from 1989, most of the ones they found had already been looted.

      Kanem-Bornu: kings on both sides of Lake Chad (about 700 to 1846 CE)

      Kanem grew up north-east of Lake Chad. In the late 1300s its kings left for Bornu, west of the lake, in today's north-eastern Nigeria, and their line, the Sayfawa, ruled there until 1846. Most early dates come from the royal chronicle, the girgam, written down long after the events, and from later histories. Many of them differ, and are labelled where they do. The sources for this chapter have so far been read only in short excerpts and still need checking against the full texts.

      about 700 (sources differ) to the 11th century: Kanem, north-east of Lake Chad

      Kanem grew up north-east of Lake Chad. Its founding is usually dated about 700, though some sources say about 600 or about 900. Its old capital, Njimi, has never been securely found; archaeologists have proposed Tié, which is not placed here. Caravans brought rock salt south from Bilma, and Kanem sent ivory and enslaved people north. The lake was not the lake on today's maps. Its level rose and fell over these centuries, and its shores moved with it.

      Disputed: Kanem's founding is usually dated to about 700, but some sources give about 600 or about 900.

      • Lake Chad (Lake). The lake between Kanem, to its north-east, and Bornu, to its west. It was never a fixed shape. Its level rose and fell over these centuries; a small lake in the Bodélé depression, north-east of today's lake, dried out only about 1,000 years ago; and since the 1960s the lake has shrunk to less than a tenth of its area then. Evidence: Hydrology and climate studies (secondary sources). Location: The dot marks today's lake, and the background draws today's outline. That is not the shoreline of any period in this chapter; no older shoreline is drawn, because none has been sourced. How sure: Approximate. Sources: Coordinates and facts for the deep-time chapter (Wikipedia place articles), Extreme fluctuations of Lake Mega-Chad and the Holocene drying of the Sahara (PNAS 112), The Rise and Fall of Africa's Great Lake.
      • Kanem (Kingdom). The first heartland of the kingdom, north-east of Lake Chad. Its capital, Njimi, has never been securely located.       about 1068 to 1259 · sources differ: The Sayfawa kings

      In the late 1000s a new line of kings, the Sayfawa, began with Hummay. His dates differ: towards 1068, 1075 to 1086, or 1085 to 1097. The royal chronicle makes him the son of the king before him. The historian Dierk Lange reads his rise as a change of dynasty, not the first turn to Islam. In the 1200s Mai Dunama Dibalemi took Kanem's power north along the caravan roads, to Kawar and the Fezzan. After his death his sons fought each other, and outlying peoples stopped paying tribute.

      Disputed: Hummay's rise is dated towards 1068, 1075-1086 or 1085-1097, and whether it marks a conversion to Islam or a change of dynasty is debated. Dunama Dibalemi's reign is given as 1210-1259 or 1221-1259.

      1376 to about 1488 · sources differ: From Kanem to Bornu

      From around Lake Fitri, to the east, came the Bulala. By one account they killed five of the six kings who reigned between 1376 and 1400. Mai Umar ibn Idris left Njimi and led the Kanembu west, to Bornu, on the far side of the lake. The move is dated from about 1380 to 1387. In Bornu the Kanembu married into the peoples already there, and from them came the Kanuri. For decades the court had no lasting seat. Then Mai Ali Gaji built Ngazargamu, between two rivers. Its founding is dated anywhere from about 1460 to 1488.

      Disputed: The Bulala are said to have taken Njimi in 1363 by one account, or to have driven the Sayfawa out by 1376 and taken Kanem by 1388 by another. The move to Bornu is dated about 1380 or about 1387, and Ngazargamu's founding from about 1460 to about 1488.

      about 1571 to 1603 · dates differ: Idris Alooma

      Bornu was at its strongest under Mai Idris Alooma. Most sources give his reign as about 1571 to 1603; others begin it in 1564 or end it as late as 1617. His chief imam, Ahmad ibn Furtu, wrote its history, in praise of the king. Ibn Furtu tells of seven expeditions against the Bulala of Kanem, about 1573 to 1578. He counts Turkish musketeers, and enslaved men of the household trained to fire guns, among the king's strengths. It is the earliest mention of guns in the region, and how much they decided is debated. Idris also made the great men of the state live at his court, and bound them to him by marriage.

      Disputed: Idris Alooma's reign is given as about 1571-1603 by most sources checked, and as about 1564-1596, about 1570 to 1600-1617, and 1580-1619 by others. The main account of his wars is his own imam's, written in his praise.

      1808 to 1846: The end of the Sayfawa

      In 1808 Fulani warriors of the jihad took Ngazargamu and destroyed it, and the capital was abandoned. Muhammad al-Amin al-Kanemi fought to free it; many stories of his part were later embellished. In 1814 he helped restore the mai, and built his own seat at Kukawa. In 1846 Mai Ibrahim called in the army of Wadai against al-Kanemi's son Umar. Umar had Ibrahim seized, and by most accounts put to death. Ibrahim's son Ali, made mai by Wadai, died the same year. With him the Sayfawa line ended, after more than seven centuries. Al-Kanemi's descendants ruled Bornu until 1893.

      Disputed: Accounts of 1846 differ: one says Umar imprisoned Ibrahim, others that he executed him (some date this to 1847); Ali is said to have died at Minarge, or to have been defeated and killed by Umar within six weeks.

      Hausa cities: walls, markets and kings (about 1000 to 1526 CE)

      Walled towns grew across the Hausa lands of today's northern Nigeria. This chapter begins with Kano. Most of its early dates come from the Kano Chronicle, a history compiled from older traditions. It counts reigns by their length, so its years are a later reckoning and are labelled that way. The copy translated in 1908 was written down in the late nineteenth century; the historian Murray Last argues its first edition dates from the mid-1600s.

      About 1000–1499 · archaeology and the Kano Chronicle: The earth becomes a city

      1. Before about 1000. Before Kano was a city, it was a hill. People worked iron on Dala.
      2. Oral tradition · no date. The Kano Chronicle remembers Barbushe, keeper of a shrine on the hill. That memory is tradition, and it has no date.
      3. 1095–1134 · Kano Chronicle reckoning. By the Chronicle's reckoning, King Gijimasu began a wall, gate by gate.
      4. Finished when? Sources differ. Who finished it? The Chronicle says Yusa, in the 1100s. Nigeria's heritage file says Zamnagawa, in the 1300s.
      5. 1463–1499 · Kano Chronicle reckoning. Then Muhammad Rumfa. The Chronicle says he built a palace and moved in the next year.
      6. 1463–1499 · Kano Chronicle reckoning. The year after, he pushed the walls outward, gate by gate.
      7. 1463–1499 · Kano Chronicle reckoning. He founded a market, Kurmi, which still trades today.
      8. 1463–1499 · Kano Chronicle reckoning. A scholar, al-Maghili, wrote Rumfa a book on how a king should rule.
      9. By 1499 · Kano Chronicle reckoning. A walled city needs more than walls. Who lived inside them?

      Disputed: Who finished Kano's first wall? The Kano Chronicle credits Yusa (1136–1194 by its reckoning); Nigeria's 2007 UNESCO tentative-list file credits Zamnagawa, in the mid-14th century. The age of the Dala settlement also differs: the 7th century (Iliffe) or the 10th (UNESCO file).

      • Kano · walled city. Kano grew around Dala hill. By the Kano Chronicle's reckoning its first wall was begun between 1095 and 1134, and Muhammad Rumfa (1463–1499) built a palace, extended the walls through named gates and founded Kurmi market. The palace site, Gidan Rumfa, is still the emir's residence, and Kurmi still trades. Schematic: Original schematic stage set of an earth-built city, not a survey or reconstruction. Each part appears at its own date (listed under What appears when). The Chronicle names the gates but does not place them, so gate positions, wall lines, the palace footprint and the market are schematic; the walls are drawn as sun-dried earth (tubali) on a sloping profile with a crenellated crest. Nothing later is added: no present-day palace decoration (mostly 1930s–40s), no 1951 mosque or minaret, no 16th-century wall line, no emblem or bridge. What appears when: Iron working on Dala: from the 7th century (Iliffe) or the 10th (UNESCO file); shown from the later date; Barbushe and the shrine on Dala: oral tradition in the Kano Chronicle, shown without a date and without his likeness or rites; First wall begun under Gijimasu, 1095–1134 (Kano Chronicle reckoning); Gate of Bazugar, named in the Chronicle; position schematic; The water gate, named in the Chronicle; position schematic; Gate of Adama, named in the Chronicle; position schematic; Rest of the first wall, dashed while its date is in question: Yusa, 1136–1194 (Chronicle) or Zamnagawa, mid-14th century (UNESCO file); First wall complete by the mid-14th century on either account; Rumfa's palace: the Chronicle's Dakin Rimfa, on the site of today's Gidan Rumfa (about 1480, ArchNet); footprint schematic, no later decoration; Courts in sequence behind the gate (processional plan, ArchNet); Round gatehouse: the older form before the early 20th century (ArchNet); Rumfa's wall from Kofar Dagachi towards Kofar Mata (Kano Chronicle); Kofar Dagachi, named in the Chronicle; position schematic; Kofar Mata, named in the Chronicle; position schematic; On to Kofar Gertawasa and Kofar Kawayi (Kano Chronicle); Kofar Gertawasa, named in the Chronicle; position schematic; Kofar Kawayi, named in the Chronicle; position schematic; Dotted: the stretch between Kofar Kawayi and Kofar Na'isa, which the Chronicle does not describe; From Kofar Na'isa to Kofar Kansakali (Kano Chronicle); Kofar Na'isa, named in the Chronicle and still identified in 2016; position schematic; Kofar Kansakali, named in the Chronicle and still identified in 2016; position schematic; Kurmi market, founded by Rumfa (Kano Chronicle); open ground, no goods named; Market stalls: simple shelters, number and form schematic; Market stalls: simple shelters, number and form schematic; Roads to the gates: schematic; Road from the north: schematic; Al-Maghili's Taj al-din, advice on kingship written for Rumfa (Verskin 2019). Evidence: The Kano Chronicle (compiled from older traditions; Palmer's 1908 translation), Nigeria's 2007 heritage file, archaeology cited by Iliffe, and architectural history. Location: Representative point for the old walled city, rounded; not a survey of the walls or gates. How sure: Approximate. Sources: Kano Chronicle, Muhammad Rumfa (with the Kano Chronicle passage on his reign, Palmer 1908), Gijimasu (with the Kano Chronicle passage on the first wall), Ancient Kano City Walls and Associated Sites (Tentative List), Dalla Hill, Gidan Rumfa.
      • Katsina (City-state). Another Hausa city, north-west of Kano, with its own king. Its rulers moved here in the fifteenth century from Durbi ta Kusheyi, and Muhammadu Korau, its first Muslim king, is credited with founding the walled town. The Kano Chronicle records that Kano's first war with Katsina came in Rumfa's reign and lasted eleven years, with neither side winning. Evidence: Kano Chronicle (Palmer 1908) and secondary sources. Location: Today's city centre, rounded. The fifteenth-century town's extent is not drawn, and the earlier seat at Durbi ta Kusheyi, about 29 km to the south-east, is not placed. How sure: Approximate. Sources: Muhammad Rumfa (with the Kano Chronicle passage on his reign, Palmer 1908), Kingdom of Katsina (Wikipedia).

      Sources: Kano Chronicle, Historical Metaphors in the Kano Chronicle, Gijimasu (with the Kano Chronicle passage on the first wall), Yusa (Tsaraki) (with the Kano Chronicle passage on the walls), Muhammad Rumfa (with the Kano Chronicle passage on his reign, Palmer 1908), Ancient Kano City Walls and Associated Sites (Tentative List), Dalla Hill, Gidan Rumfa, Kurmi Market, al-Maghili, A Survey of Styles and Functions of Kano Ancient City Wall and Gates, Kano city walls, Hausa architecture.

      1438–1526 · Kano Chronicle reckoning and Leo Africanus: Who lived inside the walls

      1. 1438–1452 · Kano Chronicle reckoning. Go back before Rumfa, to King Abdullahi Burja. People already lived inside the first wall.
      2. 1438–1452 · Kano Chronicle reckoning. The Chronicle says Burja opened roads from Bornu, in the east, to Gwanja, in the south-west.
      3. 1438–1452 · Kano Chronicle reckoning. He was the first in Hausaland to own camels.
      4. 1438–1452 · Kano Chronicle reckoning. He was also the first to send tribute to Bornu. His men raided the south for captives, and settled them in twenty-one new towns.
      5. 1452–1463 · Kano Chronicle reckoning. Under Yakubu, Fulani came from Mali with books on divinity and etymology. Salt became common in Hausaland.
      6. 1463–1499 · Kano Chronicle reckoning. Then came Rumfa: his palace, new walls through named gates, and Kurmi market.
      7. 1463–1499 · Kano Chronicle reckoning. Traders and scholars came to the city.
      8. 1463–1499 · Kano Chronicle reckoning. Rumfa gave offices of state to eunuchs, and began a council of nine, the Tara-ta-Kano.
      9. 1463–1499 · Kano Chronicle reckoning. He began kulle, the seclusion of women, and was the first to have kakaki, long royal trumpets.
      10. 1463–1499 · Kano Chronicle reckoning. In his time came Kano's first war with Katsina. It lasted eleven years, and neither side won.
      11. 1526 · Leo Africanus's account; his visit is doubted. Writing in 1526, Leo Africanus described Kano's people as wealthy merchants and skilled craftsmen. Whether he ever went there is doubted. By then, Wangara merchants had probably brought kola nuts into the trade.

      Disputed: Did Leo Africanus see Kano? Fisher (1978) doubts that he visited Hausaland at all, so his description is given as his account, not as an eyewitness record. Yakubu's reign is 1452–1463 by the Chronicle's eleven years; one summary starts it in 1432.

      • Kano · the people inside. Who lived in Kano in the fifteenth century, told from the Kano Chronicle's reigns of Abdullahi Burja (1438–1452), Yakubu (1452–1463) and Muhammad Rumfa (1463–1499), by its reckoning, and from Leo Africanus's description, written in 1526. Schematic: Carries on from the previous scene's stage set as it stood in 1438; Rumfa's palace, walls and market rise again at their own date. People, camels and goods are small schematic figures with no faces, dress or likenesses, and their numbers are illustrative. The twenty-one towns of captives are shown as a count, because their places are not known. Roads are schematic. What appears when: Rumfa's palace: the Chronicle's Dakin Rimfa, on the site of today's Gidan Rumfa (about 1480, ArchNet); footprint schematic, no later decoration; Courts in sequence behind the gate (processional plan, ArchNet); Round gatehouse: the older form before the early 20th century (ArchNet); Rumfa's wall from Kofar Dagachi towards Kofar Mata (Kano Chronicle); Kofar Dagachi, named in the Chronicle; position schematic; Kofar Mata, named in the Chronicle; position schematic; On to Kofar Gertawasa and Kofar Kawayi (Kano Chronicle); Kofar Gertawasa, named in the Chronicle; position schematic; Kofar Kawayi, named in the Chronicle; position schematic; Dotted: the stretch between Kofar Kawayi and Kofar Na'isa, which the Chronicle does not describe; From Kofar Na'isa to Kofar Kansakali (Kano Chronicle); Kofar Na'isa, named in the Chronicle and still identified in 2016; position schematic; Kofar Kansakali, named in the Chronicle and still identified in 2016; position schematic; Kurmi market, founded by Rumfa (Kano Chronicle); open ground, no goods named; Market stalls: simple shelters, number and form schematic; Market stalls: simple shelters, number and form schematic; Roads to the gates: schematic; Road from the north: schematic; Al-Maghili's Taj al-din, advice on kingship written for Rumfa (Verskin 2019); Homes inside the first wall, which was built to protect a growing population (UNESCO file); number and form schematic; Townspeople: schematic figures, with no faces or dress drawn; Road towards Bornu, which Abdullahi Burja opened, 1438–1452 (Kano Chronicle reckoning); route schematic; Road towards Gwanja, the Chronicle's name for the lands to the south-west, opened by Burja; route schematic. The Gonja state itself was founded later (Lovejoy 1978); Camels: Burja was the first in Hausaland to own them (Kano Chronicle); caravan schematic; Twenty-one towns of captives taken in raids to the south under Burja (Kano Chronicle). Their places are not known, so they are shown as a count while the Chronicle's record is told; Fulani from Mali bring books on divinity and etymology, in Yakubu's reign, 1452–1463 (Kano Chronicle reckoning); Salt becomes common in Hausaland, in Yakubu's reign (Kano Chronicle); slabs schematic; Traders at Kurmi: Rumfa's reign drew traders and scholars to Kano; figures schematic; The Tara-ta-Kano, a council of nine that Rumfa began (Kano Chronicle); nine marks with no likenesses, place schematic; Kakaki, the long metal trumpets of Hausa royal courts, which Rumfa was the first to have (Kano Chronicle); figures schematic. Evidence: The Kano Chronicle (Palmer's 1908 translation), Lovejoy (1978) on kola, and Leo Africanus's description as summarised after Fisher (1978). Location: Representative point for the old walled city, rounded; not a survey of the walls or gates. How sure: Approximate. Sources: Kano Chronicle, Abdullahi Burja (with the Kano Chronicle passage on his reign, Palmer 1908), Yakubu (with the Kano Chronicle passage on his reign, Palmer 1908), Muhammad Rumfa (with the Kano Chronicle passage on his reign, Palmer 1908), Ancient Kano City Walls and Associated Sites (Tentative List), Kano (Wikipedia), on Leo Africanus's description.
      • Katsina (City-state). Another Hausa city, north-west of Kano, with its own king. Its rulers moved here in the fifteenth century from Durbi ta Kusheyi, and Muhammadu Korau, its first Muslim king, is credited with founding the walled town. The Kano Chronicle records that Kano's first war with Katsina came in Rumfa's reign and lasted eleven years, with neither side winning. Evidence: Kano Chronicle (Palmer 1908) and secondary sources. Location: Today's city centre, rounded. The fifteenth-century town's extent is not drawn, and the earlier seat at Durbi ta Kusheyi, about 29 km to the south-east, is not placed. How sure: Approximate. Sources: Muhammad Rumfa (with the Kano Chronicle passage on his reign, Palmer 1908), Kingdom of Katsina (Wikipedia).
      • Bornu (Kingdom). The kingdom east of Kano that grew from Kanem. By the Kano Chronicle's reckoning, Abdullahi Burja (1438–1452) was the first Hausa king to send it tribute, and he opened the road from Bornu to Gwanja through Kano. Evidence: Kano Chronicle (Palmer 1908) and secondary sources. Location: Drawn at Ngazargamu, which became Bornu's capital about 1472. The point stands for the kingdom, not a city. How sure: Approximate. Sources: Bornu Empire (Wikipedia), Abdullahi Burja (with the Kano Chronicle passage on his reign, Palmer 1908).

      1349–1516 · Kano Chronicle reckoning and other sources: Hausa cities side by side

      1. Hausa tradition · the Bayajidda story. Hausa tradition tells of Bayajidda, a prince from the east. At Daura he killed the snake that guarded the well, and married the queen.
      2. Hausa tradition · the Bayajidda story. Their descendants, the story says, founded seven Hausa states. They were never one kingdom: each walled city had its own king, the sarki.
      3. Hausa tradition · the seven tasks. In the story each had its task. Kano and Rano dyed cloth with indigo, Katsina and Daura kept the markets, Gobir fought off invaders, and Zazzau supplied slaves.
      4. 1349–1385 · Kano Chronicle reckoning. The cities fought each other. Kano's king Yaji drove out the king of Rano, and Rano never ruled itself again.
      5. 1421–1438 · Kano Chronicle; others differ. The Chronicle says that in Dauda's reign Zazzau, under Queen Amina, conquered the towns as far as Kwararafa and Nupe. Other sources place her a century or more later.
      6. 1438–1452 · Kano Chronicle reckoning. Kano's Abdullahi Burja was the first Hausa king to send tribute to Bornu. Whether every city paid, or only Kano and Biram, is not known.
      7. about 1445–1495 · Katsina Chronicle; others differ. In Katsina, a cleric, Muhammadu Korau, became the first Muslim king. He is credited with the walled town that grew into Katsina city.
      8. 1463–1499 · Kano Chronicle reckoning. Kano and Katsina, the two great markets, fought for eleven years in Rumfa's reign, and neither side won.
      9. 1512–1516 · sources differ. Then Songhai's armies came from the west. Askia Muhammad attacked Katsina; how far Songhai ruled the Hausa cities is disputed.
      10. 1516 · Tarikh al-Sudan, a Timbuktu Chronicle. In 1516 Kanta of Kebbi broke with Songhai and beat the army sent against him. The Hausa cities stayed separate until the jihad of 1804.

      Disputed: Amina's dates differ by more than a century: the Kano Chronicle puts her in Dauda's reign (1421–1438), a Zaria list in the early sixteenth century, and others after 1576; her name is missing from Zazzau's king lists, and whether she was queen is disputed. Korau of Katsina is dated about 1445–1495 by the Katsina Chronicle, 1492–1541 by another list and to the thirteenth century by a local tradition. Songhai's hold on the Hausa cities is disputed: one account dates Askia's conquest of Katsina to 1512 and has Katsina a vassal until 1554, others say he also took Zazzau and Gobir, and Leo Africanus, whose visit is doubted, adds Kano.

      • Daura (City-state). Remembered in Hausa tradition as the mother city of the Hausa states: there, the story says, Bayajidda killed the snake in the Kusugu well and married Queen Daurama. By one historian's reading, tribute to Bornu was sent by way of Daura. Evidence: Oral tradition, in secondary sources. Location: Today's town of the same name. How sure: Approximate. Sources: Hausa Kingdoms (Wikipedia), Coordinates and town facts for the map key (Wikipedia place articles).
      • Kano (City-state). Kano as one Hausa state among several, each with its own king. Its Chronicle supplies most of this chapter's dates, so Kano's view of its neighbours is the one best recorded. Evidence: Kano Chronicle (Palmer 1908) and secondary sources. Location: Today's old city of Kano. How sure: Approximate. Sources: Hausa Kingdoms (Wikipedia), Coordinates and town facts for the map key (Wikipedia place articles), Kano Chronicle.
      • Katsina (City-state). Another Hausa city, north-west of Kano, with its own king. Its rulers moved here in the fifteenth century from Durbi ta Kusheyi, and Muhammadu Korau, its first Muslim king, is credited with founding the walled town. The Kano Chronicle records that Kano's first war with Katsina came in Rumfa's reign and lasted eleven years, with neither side winning. Evidence: Kano Chronicle (Palmer 1908) and secondary sources. Location: Today's city centre, rounded. The fifteenth-century town's extent is not drawn, and the earlier seat at Durbi ta Kusheyi, about 29 km to the south-east, is not placed. How sure: Approximate. Sources: Muhammad Rumfa (with the Kano Chronicle passage on his reign, Palmer 1908), Kingdom of Katsina (Wikipedia).
      • Zazzau (City-state). The southern Hausa state. Captives taken in the lands to its south were collected there and sent north to the markets of Kano and Katsina. Its best-known figure, Amina, is dated differently by different sources. Evidence: Secondary sources, and the Kano Chronicle on Amina. Location: Drawn at today's Zaria, which was founded about 1536. Zazzau's earlier capitals, such as Turunku, are not placed: the dashed ring marks the region, not a site. How sure: Approximate. Sources: Kingdom of Zazzau (Wikipedia), Coordinates for the Hausa cities scene (Wikipedia place articles), Dauda (with the Kano Chronicle passage on his reign, Palmer 1908), Amina of Zazzau (Wikipedia).
      • Gobir (City-state). The northernmost Hausa state, which tradition gives the task of war against invaders. Under Tuareg pressure from the north its people moved south more than once. Evidence: Oral tradition and secondary sources. Location: Drawn at today's Birni Lalle in Niger, inside a wide ring, because where Gobir's capital stood in these years is uncertain. Disputed: One summary makes Birnin Lalle Gobir's capital from about 1450 to 1600, but the same article's text dates the move there to the early eighteenth century, and earlier centres in Asben or at Marandet are also proposed. How sure: Disputed. Sources: Gobir (Wikipedia), Coordinates for the Hausa cities scene (Wikipedia place articles), Hausa Kingdoms (Wikipedia).
      • Rano (City-state). One of the seven Hausa states of tradition. By the Kano Chronicle's reckoning Kano's king Yaji (1349–1385) drove out its king, and Rano never regained its independence, so it is drawn faintly. Evidence: Kano Chronicle (Palmer 1908) and secondary sources. Location: Today's town of the same name. How sure: Approximate. Sources: Yaji I (with the Kano Chronicle passage on his reign, Palmer 1908), Hausa Kingdoms (Wikipedia), Coordinates for the Hausa cities scene (Wikipedia place articles).
      • Biram (City-state). The seventh Hausa state of tradition, founded by Bayajidda's son by a princess of Bornu. One historian counts it, with Kano, among the states that paid tribute to Bornu. Evidence: Oral tradition and secondary sources. Location: Drawn at today's Hadejia, which was once known as Biram. The old town of Biram itself is not placed: the dashed ring marks the area. How sure: Approximate. Sources: Hausa Kingdoms (Wikipedia), Coordinates for the Hausa cities scene (Wikipedia place articles).
      • Bornu (Kingdom). The kingdom east of Kano that grew from Kanem. By the Kano Chronicle's reckoning, Abdullahi Burja (1438–1452) was the first Hausa king to send it tribute, and he opened the road from Bornu to Gwanja through Kano. Evidence: Kano Chronicle (Palmer 1908) and secondary sources. Location: Drawn at Ngazargamu, which became Bornu's capital about 1472. The point stands for the kingdom, not a city. How sure: Approximate. Sources: Bornu Empire (Wikipedia), Abdullahi Burja (with the Kano Chronicle passage on his reign, Palmer 1908).
      • Kebbi (Kingdom). A Hausa-speaking state to the west, which tradition lists among the Banza Bakwai, seven states it ranked below the Hausa seven. In 1516 its leader Kanta rebelled against Songhai and defeated the army sent against him. Evidence: Secondary sources, resting partly on the Tarikh al-Sudan. Location: Drawn at Surame, the walled town Kanta built in the sixteenth century, to stand for Kebbi. His first capital, Birnin Leka, is not placed. How sure: Approximate. Evidence: Kano Chronicle (Palmer 1908). How sure: Approximate. Sources: Abdullahi Burja (with the Kano Chronicle passage on his reign, Palmer 1908), Hausa Kingdoms (Wikipedia).

      The Sokoto Caliphate: jihad, emirates and conquest (1804 to 1903)

      In 1804 the scholar Usman dan Fodio led a jihad against the Hausa kings. Within a few years most of the Hausa cities were ruled by emirs who owed allegiance to a caliph at Sokoto, and the caliphate grew to the Yoruba town of Ilorin in the south and Adamawa in the east. It is drawn as the caliph's seats with a line from each emirate, not as one border, because how far each emir's rule reached on the ground was never surveyed. It lasted until British forces took Kano and Sokoto in 1903. Most dates here come from encyclopedias that point to the historians they cite; where they disagree, it says so.

      1774–1809: The jihad: from Degel to Sokoto

      1. 1774–1804 · Usman at Degel. Usman dan Fodio, a Fulani scholar and preacher, lived and taught at Degel, in the Hausa kingdom of Gobir.
      2. February 1804. Gobir's king, Yunfa, turned against him. In February 1804 Usman and his community left Degel for Gudu, about 48 km to the north-west: their hijra.
      3. February 1804. At Gudu his followers named him Amir al-Mu'minin, commander of the faithful. On 21 February 1804 Yunfa declared war on him.
      4. 21 June 1804. On 21 June 1804, at the lake of Kwatto, the jihad's army defeated Yunfa's. Where the lake lay is not certain, so no place is drawn.
      5. 1805. Across Hausaland, leaders who carried Usman's flag rose against their kings. Zaria fell to the jihad in 1805.
      6. 1807. In 1807 jihad forces captured Kano, and an emirate replaced its Hausa king.
      7. 3 October 1808. On 3 October 1808 Alkalawa, Gobir's capital, fell, and Yunfa was killed.
      8. 1809. In 1809 Usman's son Muhammad Bello turned the camp at Sokoto into a town. It became the seat of the caliphate.

      Disputed: Most sources give 21 February 1804 for Yunfa's declaration of war and 21 June 1804 for the battle at Kwatto, but where the lake lay is not settled. Alkalawa's founding as Gobir's capital is dated to 1756, 1757 or the 1760s. The date Sokoto first served as the jihad's camp is also given as 1804 or 1805, with the town founded in 1809.

      • Degel. The town in the Hausa kingdom of Gobir where Usman dan Fodio lived and taught from 1774 to 1804, before the hijra to Gudu. Evidence: Secondary sources (encyclopedia). Location: Drawn at the position a city database gives for today's Degel, inside a ring: the Wikipedia article on Degel has no coordinates, and the town of 1804 has not been placed from a survey. How sure: Approximate. Sources: Degel (Wikipedia), Degel, Sokoto (Bamwor city listing).
      • Alkalawa (City-state). The walled capital of Gobir from the mid-eighteenth century. The jihad's forces took it on 3 October 1808, and Gobir's king Yunfa was killed. Evidence: Secondary sources (encyclopedia). Location: The abandoned site in today's Sabon Birni area of Sokoto State, rounded from the coordinates in the Alkalawa article. How sure: Approximate. Sources: Alkalawa (Wikipedia), Battle of Tabkin Kwatto (Wikipedia).
      • Zaria (Emirate). Zaria, capital of Zazzau, was captured in 1805 during the jihad, and became the seat of an emirate. Evidence: Secondary sources (encyclopedia). Location: Today's city of Zaria. How sure: Firm. Sources: Coordinates and town facts for the map key (Wikipedia place articles), Sokoto Caliphate (Wikipedia).
      • Kano (Emirate). Jihad forces captured Kano in 1807, and an emirate replaced its Hausa king. Evidence: Secondary sources (encyclopedia). Location: The old city of Kano. How sure: Firm. Sources: Sokoto Caliphate (Wikipedia), Coordinates and town facts for the map key (Wikipedia place articles).
      • Sokoto (Seat of the caliphate). Muhammad Bello turned the jihad's camp at Sokoto into a town in 1809. It became the seat of the caliph, the Amir al-Mu'minin. Evidence: Secondary sources (encyclopedia). Location: Today's city of Sokoto. How sure: Firm. Sources: Sokoto Caliphate (Wikipedia), Coordinates and town facts for the map key (Wikipedia place articles). Emblem: Nothing documented: Flags circulate online, but no source for any design has been found. Nothing is drawn until a description from the time or a surviving banner is found, for example in travellers' accounts such as Clapperton's or Barth's. How sure: To check.

      Sources: Sokoto Caliphate (Wikipedia), Jihad of Usman dan Fodio (Wikipedia), Degel (Wikipedia), Battle of Tabkin Kwatto (Wikipedia), Alkalawa (Wikipedia), Coordinates and town facts for the map key (Wikipedia place articles).

      1812–1841: A caliphate of emirates

      1. 1812. By 1812 Usman's brother Abdullahi ruled from Gwandu, west of Sokoto.
      2. 20 April 1817. Usman dan Fodio died at Sokoto on 20 April 1817. His son Muhammad Bello became caliph.
      3. 1817–1829 · Bello and Abdullahi. Abdullahi at first refused to recognise Bello. The caliphate came to be run in two halves: the eastern emirates answered to Sokoto, the western and southern ones to Gwandu, under the caliph.
      4. 1817–1841 · the emirates. Each emir was appointed by the caliph and ruled with wide self-rule. Every year he travelled to pledge allegiance and bring tribute: crops, cowries and enslaved people.
      5. 1823–1824 · sources differ. In the south, Afonja, who had taken Ilorin out of the Oyo empire, was killed by his allies. Abd al-Salam became Ilorin's first emir, under Gwandu.
      6. 1841. In 1841, after several moves, Modibbo Adama settled the capital of Adamawa at Yola, far to the east. He had led its jihad since 1809.

      Disputed: Gwandu's founding as an emirate is dated 1805, 1809 or 1812 by different sources; Abdullahi's rule there is dated from 1812. Ilorin's first emir is dated from 1823 or 1824. Bauchi's founding is dated 1805 by one source and to conquests between 1809 and 1818 by another.

      January 1897 to July 1903: Conquest: the caliphate falls

      From 1897 the caliphate was attacked from the south. In January 1897 a Royal Niger Company force under George Goldie took Bida, the Nupe capital, and deposed its emir; Ilorin's emir then submitted to the company. On 1 January 1900 the company handed its territories to the British government, and on paper the emirates lay inside a British protectorate. British forces took Zaria in 1901. A force under Colonel Thomas Morland left Zaria at the end of January 1903 and took Kano on 3 February after heavy fighting. Sokoto fell after a battle on 15 March. On 21 March Lugard named a new sultan, Attahiru II, and emirs who accepted British rule were kept in office under British officers. Caliph Attahiru I had left Sokoto with his followers. British forces caught up with them at Burmi, in today's Gombe State, where he and many of his followers were killed on 27 July 1903.

      Disputed: The day Goldie's force took Bida is given as 25 or 29 January 1897, and accounts differ on whether Ilorin submitted or was forced to. One source dates the battle for Sokoto to 15 March 1903, another has the caliphate's council concede to Lugard on 13 March. Attahiru I's death is dated 27 July 1903 at Burmi in most sources, but June, 29 July or August 1903 in others. Burmi itself is not placed: no checked position was found.

      • Bida (Emirate). The capital of the Nupe emirate. A Royal Niger Company force under George Goldie took it in January 1897 and deposed the emir. Colonial claim: claimed, then taken during this scene. Evidence: Secondary sources (encyclopedia) and newspaper reports of 1897. Location: Today's town of Bida, rounded. Disputed: A report of February 1897 has the company's troops advancing on Bida on 25 January; a later account has Goldie entering the town on 29 January. How sure: Disputed. Sources: Bida (Wikipedia), "The Battle of Bida", The Spectator, 13 February 1897, p. 6, Report of the Bida expedition (Papers Past, 27 March 1897), George Taubman Goldie (Wikipedia).
      • Ilorin (Emirate). Once a town of the Oyo empire. After Afonja, who had taken it out of Oyo, was killed by his allies, Abd al-Salam, son of the scholar Alimi, became its first emir and pledged allegiance to the caliphate, through Gwandu. Colonial claim: claimed, then taken during this scene. Evidence: Secondary sources (encyclopedia). Location: Rounded from the coordinates in the Ilorin Emirate article. Disputed: Afonja's death and Abd al-Salam's accession are dated 1823 in one article and 1824 in others; one ruler list gives his reign as 1824 to 1842. How sure: Disputed. Sources: Ilorin (Wikipedia), Ilorin Emirate (Wikipedia), Gwandu Emirate (Wikipedia).
      • Zaria (Emirate). Zaria, capital of Zazzau, was captured in 1805 during the jihad, and became the seat of an emirate. Colonial claim: claimed, then taken during this scene. Evidence: Secondary sources (encyclopedia). Location: Today's city of Zaria. How sure: Firm. Sources: Coordinates and town facts for the map key (Wikipedia place articles), Sokoto Caliphate (Wikipedia).
      • Kano (Emirate). Jihad forces captured Kano in 1807, and an emirate replaced its Hausa king. Colonial claim: claimed, then taken during this scene. Evidence: Secondary sources (encyclopedia). Location: The old city of Kano. How sure: Firm. Sources: Sokoto Caliphate (Wikipedia), Coordinates and town facts for the map key (Wikipedia place articles).
      • Sokoto (Seat of the caliphate). Muhammad Bello turned the jihad's camp at Sokoto into a town in 1809. It became the seat of the caliph, the Amir al-Mu'minin. Colonial claim: claimed, then taken during this scene. Evidence: Secondary sources (encyclopedia). Location: Today's city of Sokoto. How sure: Firm. Sources: Sokoto Caliphate (Wikipedia), Coordinates and town facts for the map key (Wikipedia place articles). Emblem: Nothing documented: Flags circulate online, but no source for any design has been found. Nothing is drawn until a description from the time or a surviving banner is found, for example in travellers' accounts such as Clapperton's or Barth's. How sure: To check.
      • Royal Niger Company campaign against Bida and Ilorin. Military campaign: Bida (Jan 1897 (month only)) to Ilorin (1897 (year only)). In January 1897 a Royal Niger Company force led by George Goldie took Bida and deposed the Nupe emir. It then marched to Ilorin, whose emir submitted and signed a treaty with the company. Evidence: Secondary sources (encyclopedia) and newspaper reports of 1897. Location: A straight line from Bida to Ilorin in the order the towns were brought under the company. The column's route is not shown. Disputed: Accounts differ on Ilorin: one says the emir hurried to submit and sign a treaty, another that its leaders were made to surrender by force. The day of Ilorin's submission has not been found, so only the year is given. How sure: Disputed. Sources: George Taubman Goldie (Wikipedia), "The Battle of Bida", The Spectator, 13 February 1897, p. 6, Report of the Bida expedition (Papers Past, 27 March 1897), Encyclopaedia Britannica (1911), vol. 19, "Niger Company".
      • British campaign from Zaria to Kano and Sokoto. Military campaign: Zaria (approx. taken 1901 (year only)) to Kano (3 Feb 1903) to Sokoto (15 Mar 1903). British forces took Zaria in 1901. A force under Colonel Thomas Morland left Zaria at the end of January 1903 and took Kano on 3 February. British forces under Kemball and Morland then took Sokoto after a battle on 15 March. Evidence: Secondary sources (encyclopedia). Location: Straight lines join the towns in the order they were taken. The columns' routes are not shown, and the line from Kano to Sokoto stands for the British advance, not one column's march. Disputed: One source dates the battle for Sokoto to 15 March 1903; another says the caliphate's council conceded to Lugard's demands on 13 March. How sure: Disputed. Sources: Coordinates and town facts for the map key (Wikipedia place articles), Battle of Kano (Wikipedia), Battle of Sokoto (Wikipedia), Colonial history of Northern Nigeria (Wikipedia).

      Colonial Nigeria: rule, railways and ports (1861 to 1960)

      After the Sokoto Caliphate fell, all of today's Nigeria came under British rule. This chapter follows how: Lagos annexed in 1861, a company ruling the Niger, conquest and the resistance to it, and the railways and ports built to carry coal and farm produce to the sea, until independence in 1960. Railways are drawn as schematic lines between the towns their sources name, when each part opened, not as the route of the track.

      How to read this map. Each scene is told in dated beats; the year shows each beat's own date. Hatched discs are claims on paper and solid ones are places held, as in the map key. The trains, steamers and moving water are decoration: they show that a line or port is open, not a timetable or a count of shipping. The scenes about conquest stay calm, with no sparks.

      1861 to 1900: A colony at Lagos, a company on the Niger

      1. August 1861. In August 1861 a British naval force entered Lagos and annexed it as a colony.
      2. 1884 and 1885. In 1884 Britain proclaimed a protectorate along the Oil Rivers, run from Calabar, and in 1885 the Berlin Conference recognised its claim.
      3. 1886 to 1899. From 1886 the Royal Niger Company ruled much of the land along the Niger and the Benue above Lokoja, under a charter.
      4. 1 January 1900. On 1 January 1900 it handed its territories to the British government, which made them the protectorates of Northern and Southern Nigeria.
      • Lagos (Port). Annexed as a British colony in August 1861; from 1906 the seat of government, and the capital at independence in 1960. Its harbour opened to ocean-going ships in 1913, and the wharf at Apapa became the end of the western railway from 1919. Colonial claim: held (solid). Evidence: Secondary sources (encyclopedia). Location: From the place article's coordinates. How sure: Firm. Sources: Lagos Colony (Wikipedia), Apapa Port Complex (Wikipedia), Federation of Nigeria (Wikipedia), Coordinates for the colonial chapter (place articles) (Wikipedia).
      • Calabar (Port). A seaport since the 16th century, for palm oil and, during the Atlantic slave trade, enslaved people. Headquarters of the British administration of the Niger Delta until 1906. Colonial claim: claimed on paper (hatched). Evidence: Secondary sources (encyclopedia). Location: From the place article's coordinates. How sure: Firm. Sources: Calabar (Wikipedia).
      • Lokoja. Where the Niger and the Benue meet. Above it, along both rivers, the Royal Niger Company had access but no effective control. Colonial claim: claimed on paper (hatched). Evidence: Secondary sources (encyclopedia). Location: From the place article's coordinates. How sure: Firm. Sources: Nigeria: a country study, "Extension of British Control" (Library of Congress, 1991), Coordinates for the colonial chapter (place articles) (Wikipedia).

      Sources: Lagos Colony (Wikipedia), Colonial Nigeria (Wikipedia), Nigeria: a country study, "Extension of British Control" (Library of Congress, 1991), Royal Niger Company (Wikipedia), Calabar (Wikipedia).

      1897 to 1906: Conquest and resistance

      1. 1897 to 1906. British rule was imposed by force, and it was resisted.
      2. February 1897. On 9 February 1897 a British force invaded the Kingdom of Benin. Benin City was looted and burned, the Benin Bronzes were carried off, and the oba, Ovonramwen, was sent into exile.
      3. 1901 to 1902. In 1901 and 1902 British forces fought the Aro Confederacy and invaded Arochukwu.
      4. 1906. In 1906 a Mahdist rising broke out at Satiru, a village outside Sokoto.
      • Benin City. Capital of the Kingdom of Benin, invaded by a British force in February 1897. Evidence: Secondary sources (encyclopedia). Location: From the place article's coordinates. How sure: Firm. Sources: Benin Expedition of 1897 (Wikipedia), Coordinates for the colonial chapter (place articles) (Wikipedia).
      • Arochukwu. Centre of the Aro Confederacy, invaded by British forces in 1901 to 1902. Evidence: Secondary sources (encyclopedia). Location: From the place article's coordinates. How sure: Firm. Sources: Anglo-Aro War (Wikipedia), Coordinates for the colonial chapter (place articles) (Wikipedia).
      • Satiru, outside Sokoto. A village outside Sokoto where a Mahdist rising broke out in 1906. Evidence: Secondary sources (encyclopedia). Location: The village is not placed: it is drawn at Sokoto inside a ring, since the source says only that it lay outside the city. How sure: Approximate. Sources: Muhammadu Attahiru II (Wikipedia), Coordinates and town facts for the map key (Wikipedia place articles).

      1896 to 1916: Iron roads to the north

      1. 1896 to 1901. The railway began at Lagos. Building started in March 1896, and trains ran to Ibadan from March 1901.
      2. 1907 to 1911. In the north, the protectorate built its own line from Baro, a port on the Niger, to Kano, between 1907 and 1911.
      3. 1911 and 1912. In 1911 the line from Lagos reached Minna and met it, and in 1912 the two became one railway.
      4. 1911 or 1916 · sources differ. Where it crossed the Niger at Jebba, a ferry carried the trains while the bridges were built; the line is said to have reached Jebba in 1916.

      1909 to 1916: Coal, and a port to ship it

      1. 1909. In 1909 the geologist Albert Kitson found coal under the village of Enugwu Ngwo, in the Udi area: coal laid down in swamps about 70 million years before.
      2. 1912 to 1913. To ship it, building began in 1912 on a port, on land the people of Diobu were made to cede; in August 1913 Lugard named it Port Harcourt.
      3. 1913 to 1916. The eastern railway was built from Port Harcourt to the coal at Enugu between 1913 and 1916.
      • Enugu coal. Coal found in 1909 under the village of Enugwu Ngwo in the Udi area, confirmed as worth mining by 1913. It formed in the swamps of about 70 million years ago told in the deep-time chapter. Evidence: Secondary sources (encyclopedia). Location: From the place article's coordinates. How sure: Firm. Sources: Enugu (Wikipedia), Port Harcourt (Wikipedia).

      1902 to 1917: One colony

      1. 1902 to 1916. Northern Nigeria was ruled from Zungeru, from 1902 until 1916.
      2. 1906. In 1906 Lagos Colony was merged into Southern Nigeria, and the seat of government moved from Calabar to Lagos.
      3. 1912 to 1914. Lugard returned in 1912 to merge the two protectorates, and in 1914 they were combined as the Colony and Protectorate of Nigeria.
      4. 1917. The north's capital moved from Zungeru to Kaduna, its capital from 1917.

      1913 to 1964: Harbours, junctions and independence

      1. 1913 to 1919. In 1913 dredging and two stone moles opened Lagos harbour to ocean-going ships, and from 1919 a wharf at Apapa was the end of the western railway.
      2. 1927 to 1932. In 1927 the eastern line was carried north through Kafanchan to Kaduna, joining the two railways, and in 1932 a railway bridge crossed the Benue at Makurdi.
      3. 1930. In the north-east the line from Kano reached Nguru in 1930.
      4. 1958 to 1964. The eastern line was carried on through Bauchi to Maiduguri between 1958 and 1964.
      5. 1 October 1960. On 1 October 1960 Nigeria became independent, with its capital at Lagos.

      The Civil War: from independence to 1970 (1960 to 1970)

      Nigeria became independent in 1960 as a federation of three regions. Six years later two coups and the killing of thousands of Igbo people in the north led the Eastern Region to declare itself the Republic of Biafra, and a civil war followed from 1967 to 1970. Most of those who died were civilians, many of them children, who starved under a blockade. This chapter is told plainly and calmly: no effects play over killing, hunger or flight.

      How to read this map. Each scene is told in dated beats; the year shows each beat's own date. Places are marked on the dates the sources give; a captured town is a point, never a filled area, and no front lines are drawn between dated places. Numbers of the dead and the displaced appear only as the ranges the sources give, never as counters, and estimates that disagree are given separately.

      1960 to 1963: A federation of regions

      1. 1 October 1960. Nigeria became independent on 1 October 1960 as a federation of three regions, the North, the West and the East, each with its own government.
      2. June 1963. In June 1963 a fourth, the Mid-Western Region, was formed from the West, with its capital at Benin City.
      3. 1 October 1963. On 1 October 1963 Nigeria became a republic, with Nnamdi Azikiwe as its first president.
      • Lagos. The federal capital at independence. Evidence: Secondary sources (encyclopedia). Location: From the place article's coordinates. How sure: Firm. Sources: Federation of Nigeria (Wikipedia), Coordinates for the colonial chapter (place articles) (Wikipedia).
      • Kaduna. Capital of the Northern Region, where the Northern Premier, Ahmadu Bello, was killed in January 1966. Evidence: Secondary sources (encyclopedia). Location: From the place article's coordinates. How sure: Firm. Sources: Kaduna (Wikipedia), 1966 Nigerian coup d'état (Wikipedia).
      • Western Region. One of the three regions at independence. Evidence: Secondary sources (encyclopedia). Location: A label placed at Ibadan. The region is not outlined, and its capital is not claimed here. How sure: Approximate. Sources: First Nigerian Republic (Wikipedia), Coordinates for the colonial chapter (place articles) (Wikipedia).
      • Eastern Region. One of the three regions at independence; declared independent as Biafra on 30 May 1967. Evidence: Secondary sources (encyclopedia). Location: A label placed at Enugu. The region is not outlined. How sure: Approximate. Sources: First Nigerian Republic (Wikipedia), Nigerian Civil War (Wikipedia), Coordinates for the colonial chapter (place articles) (Wikipedia).

Evidence: Secondary sources (encyclopedia). Location: From the place article's coordinates. How sure: Firm. Sources: Mid-Western Region, Nigeria (Wikipedia), Nigerian Civil War (Wikipedia), Coordinates for the colonial chapter (place articles) (Wikipedia).

      January 1966 to May 1967: Coups and killings

      1. 15 January 1966. On 15 January 1966 soldiers led by Kaduna Nzeogwu and four others killed 22 people, among them the Prime Minister, Abubakar Tafawa Balewa, and the Northern Premier, Ahmadu Bello.
      2. 29 July 1966. On the night of 29 July 1966 northern soldiers mutinied in a counter-coup; the head of state, Johnson Aguiyi-Ironsi, was killed at Ibadan, and Yakubu Gowon became head of state.
      3. May to October 1966. From May 1966, and most of all after 29 September, Igbo people and other easterners living in the north were massacred. Estimates of the dead range from 8,000 to 30,000, and more than a million fled to the east.
      4. January to 30 May 1967. Federal and Eastern leaders met at Aburi, in Ghana, in January 1967. On 27 May Gowon divided Nigeria into twelve states, and on 30 May Ojukwu declared the Eastern Region independent as the Republic of Biafra.
      • Lagos. The federal capital at independence. Evidence: Secondary sources (encyclopedia). Location: From the place article's coordinates. How sure: Firm. Sources: Federation of Nigeria (Wikipedia), Coordinates for the colonial chapter (place articles) (Wikipedia).

      • Ibadan. Where the head of state, Johnson Aguiyi-Ironsi, was killed in the counter-coup of July 1966. Evidence: Secondary sources (encyclopedia). Location: From the place article's coordinates. How sure: Firm. Sources: 1966 Nigerian counter-coup (Wikipedia), Coordinates for the colonial chapter (place articles) (Wikipedia).
      • Enugu. Biafra's first capital, where independence was declared on 30 May 1967; taken by federal troops on 4 October 1967. Evidence: Secondary sources (encyclopedia). Location: From the place article's coordinates. How sure: Firm. Sources: Nigerian Civil War (Wikipedia), Umuahia (Wikipedia), Enugu (Wikipedia).

      6 July 1967 to 19 May 1968: The war: 1967 to 1968

      1. 6 to 14 July 1967. The war began on 6 July 1967, when federal troops advanced into Biafra in two columns. Nsukka fell on 14 July.
      2. August to 22 September 1967. In August Biafran forces crossed into the Mid-West, through Benin City, until they were stopped at Ore on 21 August. Federal forces retook Benin City on 22 September.
      3. 4 October 1967. On 4 October federal troops took Enugu, Biafra's capital, and Ojukwu moved his government to Umuahia.
      4. 5 to 7 October 1967. At Asaba, on 5 to 7 October, federal soldiers killed civilians. Estimates of the dead range from 500 to 800.
      5. 17 October 1967 to 19 May 1968. Calabar was invaded from 17 October, and Port Harcourt was taken on 19 May 1968. Biafra was surrounded.
      • Nsukka. Taken by federal troops on 14 July 1967, in the first week of the war. Evidence: Secondary sources (encyclopedia). Location: From the place article's coordinates. How sure: Firm. Sources: Nigerian Civil War (Wikipedia), Coordinates for the civil-war chapter (place articles) (Wikipedia).

Location: From the place article's coordinates. How sure: Firm. Sources: Nigerian Civil War (Wikipedia), Umuahia (Wikipedia), Enugu (Wikipedia).
